How many shrimp get crushed in the net?

Trawlers catch enormous numbers of wild shrimp every year. On the way up from the sea floor the catch piles up in the bag at the end of the net and presses down on itself, and some shrimp are crushed: their shell cracks, or a neighbour's spine pierces it. We found no research that calculates how many. We built a computer model of that pressure to estimate what share of the catch is crushed in seven fisheries, and at which stage of the haul it happens. Every crushing percentage on this page is a model estimate, not a measurement, and crushed does not necessarily mean dead.

The stages of a haul, filmed on different boats. Each picture opens its film at that moment. The model covers the first five stages and treats a bin like a pile on deck. It stops before sorting and killing (stages 7 and 8).

The short answerHow the model worksResultsHow sure are we?What we can't say yetWhat would helpAbout this workThe details

The short answer

Big trawler catches come out highest

In Greenland and Norway, large trawlers pull their catch up a ramp at the back of the boat. There the model's best estimate is that 64% and 47% of the catch is crushed. Smaller catches come out far lower: 13% for US Gulf shrimp and 2% in small research hauls of seabob shrimp off Brazil.

In big catches, most of it happens out of the water

Under water, the water holds up most of the catch's weight. Once the bag leaves the water that support is gone: in the model a northern prawn presses down about 39 times harder in air. With default settings, most crushing on the big stern trawlers happens while the bag is pulled up the ramp and lies closed on deck. In the small brown shrimp and Gulf shrimp catches the tow matters more.

The ranking is firmer than the percentages

Greenland comes out most crushed in all 192 versions of the model we tried. That rests partly on catch sizes borrowed from Canadian trawlers. Norwegian trawlers report smaller catches in Greenland waters, which would give a lower figure. For Norway the best estimate is 47%. After weighting the versions by the field studies, the middle 90% of their results runs from 27% to 75%, and single hauls vary around each version's result.

How the model works

Picture the catch in the bag as a stack of 50 slices, like pancakes. At each stage of the haul the model weighs the stack, works out the pressure on each slice, turns that into a push on a single shrimp, and checks whether the push is stronger than the shrimp's shell.

Many inputs are uncertain, such as the size of the catch or the strength of a shell. For most of them we set a lower limit, a best guess and an upper limit. The computer then plays out each fishery's haul 10,000 times, and each time it draws a value for every uncertain input at random between its limits. Many inputs favour values near the best guess; some give every value an equal chance. Catch size works differently: its limits hold 9 hauls in 10, so some draws fall outside them. For one version of the model, the result is the average over its simulated hauls, with big hauls counting for more because they hold more shrimp. How sure are we? explains how the 192 versions are combined into the best estimate.

How heavy is the catch?

Weigh the catch in the bag, stage by stage. Under water it almost floats; out of water it is heavy.

Pressure on each slice

The slices at the bottom carry the weight of all the slices above, like the bottom book in a stack.

Force on one shrimp

Turn the slice's pressure into a push on one shrimp. In a pile a few shrimp carry far more than their share, so each shrimp gets a random share of the load.

Strong enough?

Compare that push with how hard you need to squeeze this shrimp's shell to break it.

Count

If the push is stronger than the shell, the shrimp counts as crushed. Repeat for every simulated haul and average.

How hard each stage presses (Norway, default settings)

The pressure at the bottom of the pile at each stage, with every input at its best guess. The ramp presses hardest because the bag is out of the water and the model takes it to lie as deep as half its width, an upper bound. Model

With default settings, on trawlers with a ramp most crushing happens in the ramp stage. Where the bag is lifted over the side, the lift matters most, except for small catches (brown shrimp, Gulf shrimp), where the tow matters more because the loads out of water are small.

How sure are we?

We found no measurements of seven things about how a pile of shrimp behaves, so we ran the model with every combination of them: 192 versions in all. The seven unknowns, with the names used on the buttons below:

  • Load patterns: how many times the pile rearranges at each stage, once or four times;
  • Force rule: whether the pressure reaches a shrimp across its whole side, or only through the few points where neighbours touch it (the lever-arm rule);
  • Weakening: whether a shell held under load for a long time gets weaker;
  • Ramp load: how deep the bag lies on the ramp;
  • Lift width: how wide the bag hangs from the crane;
  • Spine rule: how many shrimp have a neighbour's spine pressing on them;
  • Uneven load: how unevenly the pile shares its load between shrimp.

Six have two options and one has three, which gives 192 versions. Each dot below is one version's average share crushed. Press a button to split the dots by that unknown and see how much it matters.

Split by

Dark dot: fits the five field studies wellPale dot: fits them badlyOrange mark: default settings

What the dots show

  1. The spread inside one fishery is wide. For Norway, the middle half of the 192 results fall between 41% and 72%. The measurements we have are not enough to pick one version.
  2. Two unknowns move the results most: how often the pile rearranges, and how pressure reaches a single shrimp. With four rearrangements per stage Norway's middle result is 70%, against 44% with one. With pressure passed only through the points where neighbours touch (the lever-arm rule) it is 44%, against 67% across the whole side. How deep the bag lies on the ramp (47% against 67%) and how wide it hangs from the crane (64% against 48%) come next. No single unknown decides the result, because the others can push the same way or cancel out. How unevenly the pile shares its load makes little difference to the middle result (55 to 58%), although it matters more in some versions.
  3. The field studies count most against the highest results. We compared every version with five field studies of small hauls that counted damaged or dead animals, four on shrimp and prawns and one on Norway lobster. Versions that match the studies count for more in our best estimate. The studies favour one rearrangement per stage, the lever-arm rule and fewer spine contacts, each by about two to one (64%, 67% and 63% of the weight). They rule out no option entirely, so they narrow the range but do not tell us which version is right. How the weighting works.
  4. The order of the fisheries barely changes. Greenland is first in all 192. North Sea brown shrimp and US Gulf shrimp swap places in 112 of the 192 versions, so treat them as tied. Argentina and US ocean shrimp swap in 2. In this run Argentina never comes out above Norway.

What we can't say yet

Whether crushed shrimp die

Crushed here means a cracked or pierced shell. The model does not say how badly a shrimp is hurt, or whether it dies.

What happens after the deck

The model stops at the deck. Sorting, time in air, heat, low oxygen and the killing step are not in it. The measurements we found suggest they matter a lot: in a lab test at 23 to 30 °C, most Gulf shrimp no longer appeared normal after 15 minutes in air. The evidence.

How strong a live shell is

We found no published test in which a whole live shrimp of these species was squeezed until it broke. Our starting figure is our own reading of a peeling study on chilled, headless whiteleg shrimp, plus an adjustment of our own for a slow squeeze; the study does not report a breaking force. This is the biggest gap in the model.

How a full bag really lies

We found no published measurement of a full bag of shrimp on a ramp, on deck or hanging from a crane, so the ramp angle and the shape of the hanging bag are our guesses.

What would help

Measurements that need no harm to any animal:

  • published tests of shell or body strength by species and moult stage (how recently the shrimp shed its old shell);
  • photos or video of the bag on the ramp and hanging from the crane, with something of known size in view;
  • counts of cracked and pierced shrimp as the bag is opened, by catch size, in catch that is already landed;
  • counts of live and dead shrimp at the killing step, with clock times and temperature.

About this work

Arda Enfiyeci built this model with mentoring from Jan Gaida during the Sentient Futures Project Incubator in fall 2026. It is one part of a wider look at changes on shrimp trawlers that could reduce suffering, such as shorter tows and stunning before cooking.

Much of the model code was written by OpenAI's Codex, and this page was drafted with Anthropic's Claude, both under our direction and review. The results come from the model version of 27 October 2026 and will change as real measurements come in. We also tried a simulation that follows every prawn in a pile; it is not yet reliable enough to use, so none of its results are on this page.

Words used here

Codend
The closed bag at the very end of a trawl net. The catch piles up in it.
Stern ramp
A slope at the back of big trawlers. The full bag is pulled up it onto the deck.
Lift
Lifting the bag into the air with a crane, over a hatch or a bin.
Crushed
The shell cracked under a broad squeeze, or was pierced by a neighbour's spine. Crushed does not mean dead.
kPa
A unit of pressure. 1 kPa is about the weight of a 10 cm layer of water resting on you.
N (newton)
A unit of force. 1 N is about the weight of a 100 g apple in your hand.
Simulated haul
One run of the model through a whole haul, with every uncertain input drawn at random from its range.
Version
One way of settling the seven unknowns we found no measurements for, for example which force rule to use. There are 192 versions.
Default settings
Each of the seven unknowns at our preferred option. The orange tick in the results chart and the chart of where crushing happens use them. They give the default result.
Best estimate
The middle of the 192 versions' results, each counted by how well it matches the field studies. The numbers in The short answer are best estimates.
Shell strength
How hard you have to squeeze a shrimp before its shell cracks.
Uneven-load factor
In a pile, a few shrimp carry far more than their share of the load. The model gives each shrimp a random factor for this.
Solid fraction
How much of a pile is actually shrimp. The rest is gaps full of water or air.
Rostrum
The pointed spike on a shrimp's head.
Fit weight
How well one version matches five field studies of small hauls: 1 if its average sits inside every field figure, falling towards 0 the further outside it lands. Our best estimate counts each version by this weight.
Stricter Salini check
Keeping only the versions whose average crushes less than the damage counted in one Australian field study (Salini et al. 2000), plus a margin for sampling error (two standard errors). 62 of 192 pass. It appears under Best estimate and field checks as a comparison.
Alive at kill
The share of all kept shrimp reaching the killing step (cooker, freezer, ice or stunner) that still show any sign of life.

The model, step by step

Each step shows what happens on the boat, what the model works out, what it assumes, and the main inputs with their sources. The full input sheet has 240 rows; these are the ones that matter most.

Measured someone measured it on this species or in this fishery Worked out we calculated it from measured or reported numbers Borrowed measured on a different animal, fishery or material, and used here as a stand-in Our guess we found no measurement, so we chose a value Model a result of our model, not a measurement

Step by step

Steps A and B happen once. Stages 1 to 5 follow the bag through the haul and match the pictures at the top of the page. Steps C to E are the crush test, done at every stage.

ADraw the uncertain inputs

We do not know most inputs exactly. So for each simulated haul the model draws every uncertain input at random from its range, runs once, and repeats this 10,000 times.

What a range is: each uncertain input has three values in our input sheet: a low end, a best guess and a high end. In every simulated haul the model draws a fresh value for each. For most inputs the draw always lies between the low and the high end, and how the draws spread depends on the input. For many, most draws land near the best guess and few near the ends (a hump). For some, every value in the range is equally likely (flat). The catch per bag is the exception: its low and high ends are set so that 9 hauls in 10 fall between them, and about one in ten lands outside. The chart under this step draws the main ranges.

What the model works out: a crushed share for each simulated haul. It reports the average and the spread of those results.

What it assumes

  • every input is drawn on its own, as if none were connected, except that a heavier shrimp also gets a larger body.
  • "this haul was unusually big" and "we don't know the true value" are mixed into the same draw.

Numbers it uses

Simulated hauls per fishery10,000a setting of the model, enough to make the average steady from one run to the next. It does not make the model more correct.
Slices of the catch50a setting of the model

What it can't do here

It can't tell apart real differences between hauls and our own lack of knowledge. Both end up in one wide range.

The shaded shape shows where the draws land: tall where they land often, low where they land rarely. Each row's height is set to its own peak, so heights show shape only.

BShape the bag

IllustrationA drawing of the bag at the end of the net (the codend). It shows the idea, not a model result.

The catch fills the bag at the end of the net. The model treats the bag as a round tube and the catch as a stack of 50 equal slices, like 50 pancakes.

What the model works out: how wide the bag is and how tall the stack is.

What it assumes

  • the bag is one round tube, the same width all along.
  • the catch is spread evenly; every slice holds the same number of shrimp.
  • the catch is all shrimp. No fish, stones or weed.
  • out of the water, the bag keeps its underwater width unless a setting says otherwise (see stages 3 and 4).

Numbers it uses

Catch in one bag, Norway1,834 kg (882 to 3,814)Worked outour fit to the catch reports of prawn trawl hauls in the Norwegian logbooks, ERS 2024 and ERS 2025 (zip downloads), weighted by catch
Catch in one bag, Greenland3,000 kg (1,000 to 11,000)BorrowedCanadian offshore fleet, Araya-Schmidt et al. 2023, Table 2 (2,582 to 10,982 kg per codend)
Widest the bag can open, Norway2.8 mWorked out250 meshes × 35 mm ÷ π, from the net described in Jacques et al. 2021, which we have not yet linked
Pile density in water400 kg/m³Worked outan approximate figure from the report's holding-tank advice, not a weighed density measurement: a litre of packed prawns weighs about 0.4, so 75 L holds about 30 kg, Larssen and Dyb 2009, Møreforsking Å0902, printed pp. 32 to 33

Northern prawn body density1,052 kg/m³MeasuredLucca and Warren 2024, Table 2

What it can't do here

We found no published measurement of a bag of shrimp on a ramp, on deck or hanging from a crane. The model has no bycatch, and it does not let the catch build up over the hours of the tow.

1Tow

▶

Film stillInside a shrimp trawl under water · Notus Electronics film, from 9:59

The net is dragged along for hours. Water rushing through pushes the shrimp to the back of the bag. Under water a shrimp almost floats, so the pile is light.

What the model works out: the pressure on each slice: the push of the water, plus a little weight. It is highest at the very back of the bag.

1.9 kPaNorway, back of the bag. About 19 cm of water standing on you. Model

What it assumes

  • the water's push spreads evenly through the pile.
  • every shrimp lies side-on to the push, although the push runs along the bag.
  • only the load at the end of the tow counts. Tow length changes nothing unless the weakening option is on.

Numbers it uses

Tow speed, Norway1.59 m/sMeasured3.0 to 3.2 knots in the Barents Sea, Larsen et al. 2022
Water drag number1.4 (1.06 to 2.24)Borrowedfish codends, O'Neill et al. 2005, Table 1 (paywalled)
Tow length, Norway7.0 h (4.6 to 10.3)Worked outfrom the same Norwegian logbooks; used only by the weakening option
Seawater density1,025 kg/m³MeasuredPriour, Herrmann and O'Neill 2009, author PDF p. 5

What it can't do here

It does not let the catch build up slowly, does not swing the bag, and has no picture of the real net shape.

The full bag floats at the surface for a few minutes before it comes aboard. It is still in water, so it is still light.

What the model works out: the weight of the floating pile, times a wave factor.

0.15 kPaNorway. Almost nothing: about 1.5 cm of water. Model

What it assumes

  • waves are just a number between 1 and 2 that multiplies the weight. Nothing actually moves.
  • the catch still floats, so it weighs almost nothing.

3Ramp

▶

Film stillTwo catch bags coming up the ramp at the back of the Norwegian factory trawler Remøy, 2019 (Eirik Remøy) · film, from 4:24.

On big stern trawlers (Norway, Greenland) the full bag is winched up a sloping ramp and then lies on deck. Out of the water, each northern prawn presses down about 39 times harder than it did under water.

What the model works out: two loads, and keeps the bigger one: the weight of the catch sliding down the slope, and the weight of the bag lying flat on deck.

6.3 kPaNorway. The biggest load of the whole haul: about 64 cm of water on you. Model

What it assumes

  • the ramp is tilted at 35°. We found no published ramp angle.
  • the bag lying on deck is as deep as half its underwater width. This is an upper bound, because a real bag flattens. The other option counts the slope only.
  • the whole catch goes up in one bag. It only splits if the catch is over 10 tonnes.
  • the rubbing between net and ramp is taken by the rope, not by the shrimp.

Numbers it uses

Ramp angle35° (20 to 45)Our guesswe found no measurement
Bag splits above10 t (5 to 15)Our guessour own estimate from winch ratings of 12 to 30 t; no public source
How deep the bag lieshalf its width, or slope onlyOur guessone of the seven unknowns

What it can't do here

We found no measurement of a ramp. Counting the slope only takes Norway from 47% to 29% crushed (our model estimate). The Remøy film shows the bags reach the deck in about 19 to 23 seconds, but it does not let us measure the angle or how flat the bag lies.

4Lift

▶

Film stillBag hanging over the hatch while water washes the shrimp into a tank below · Royal Greenland film, from 2:14

The bag is lifted into the air by a crane. On boats without a ramp this is the only way the catch comes aboard.

What the model works out: the pressure in a hanging bag with a rule made for grain in a silo: the walls hold up part of the weight, so the pressure stops growing at the bottom.

5.0 kPaNorway, bottom of the hanging bag. About 51 cm of water on you. Model

What it assumes

  • the hanging bag keeps its underwater width, so it is short and fat. The other option halves the width.
  • the net rubs on the catch like the wooden walls of a grain silo.
  • the bag does not swing, jerk or drop.

Numbers it uses

Silo wall friction0.15 (0 to 0.3)Borrowedwheat on wood, Janssen 1895, in Sperl's 2006 translation, pp. 4 to 5
How wide the hanging bag isfull or half its towed widthOur guessone of the seven unknowns

What it can't do here

A narrower hanging bag is taller and crushes more: half the width raises US ocean shrimp from 15% to 37% and North Sea brown shrimp from 8% to 20% (our model estimate).

The bag is opened and the catch lies in a pile or a bin before sorting.

What the model works out: the weight of the pile above each slice, as if the catch were spread flat over the deck or bin floor.

CForce on one shrimp

In a pile, most shrimp carry little of the load and a few carry much more than their share.

What the model works out: force on one shrimp = slice pressure × the shrimp's side area ÷ how much of the pile is shrimp × an uneven-load factor.

What it assumes

  • every shrimp lies on its side.
  • within one simulated haul, every shrimp in a fishery is the same size; only shell strength differs between animals.
  • the uneven-load factor is drawn again at every stage, as if the pile were reshuffled each time. One of the seven unknowns draws it four times per stage.
  • loads are shared as unevenly in a shrimp pile as in a layer of flat plastic discs.

Numbers it uses

Northern prawn side area6.3 cm² (4.4 to 8.2)Worked outfrom carapace width (Araya-Schmidt et al. 2023) and a length to weight relationship, our own calculation
Spread of the uneven-load factorgamma shape 2 (1, 2 and 4 tried)Borrowedflat plastic discs, Bililign et al. 2019, data set
Lever-arm rule (the other force rule)about ⅔ of the forceWorked outour own calculation from the physics of granular materials, no public source: a northern prawn's effective area falls from 6.3 to 4.2 cm²

What it can't do here

We found no measurement of the force on a shrimp inside a codend. How unevenly the load is shared comes from plastic discs.

DShell strength

▶

Film stillNorthern prawns on a belt (Aleksandr Lyubimov) · Barents Sea film, from 10:19

Each shrimp's shell can take some squeezing before it cracks. Big shrimp are stronger. Freshly moulted shrimp are soft.

What the model works out: a breaking force for each shrimp. A shrimp can also be pierced by a neighbour's spine, which takes much less force.

7.1 NNorthern prawn, hard shell, best guess: 17 N × (4.36 ÷ 10.6)0.66 × 0.75. It is only as reliable as the 17 N starting figure, which is our judgement. Like holding a 720 g bag of sugar on it. Worked out

What it assumes

  • the 17 N starting point fits all shrimp. It comes from one processing study: headless whiteleg shrimp of 10.6 g, chilled at 1 °C for 15 minutes until they "passed out", then kneaded between two moving belts to loosen the shell for peeling. The paper prints no breaking force; it scores how badly shells broke.
  • strength grows with size the way it does in crab claws.
  • northern prawn shells are 25% weaker than whiteleg shrimp shells. This is our judgement.
  • temperature, time out of water and being alive or dead make no difference to strength.

Numbers it uses

Thin-shell factor, prawns0.75 (0.6 to 0.9)Our guessour judgement; we found no measurement to use
Half-hard shell× 0.55 (0.3 to 0.8)Borrowedcrabs, Hicks and Johnson 1999 and Dutil et al. 2000
Soft, just moulted× 0.2 (0.1 to 0.35)Borrowedmeasured in brown shrimp with a needle test, CRANMAN final report 2022, chapter d; borrowed for the other species
Share of prawns moulting1.5% soft, 10% half-hardBorroweda related prawn, Yuriev and Korneychuk 2019, p. 106

Load a spine carries35% (20 to 60)Our guessbased on our working notes

What it can't do here

We found no published test in which a whole live shrimp of any of these species was squeezed until it broke. We will not run such a test, because it would harm animals. What would help lists measurements that need no harm.

ECrushed or not

If the force on a shrimp is bigger than its shell strength, it counts as crushed, at the first stage where that happens.

What the model works out: the share of shrimp crushed at each stage, and in total. For the default result, big hauls count for more because they hold more shrimp.

The model also has an optional step that turns crushed shrimp into deaths, using a Norway lobster study. It is not used here, because we found no data on how many crushed shrimp go on to die.

What it assumes

  • a shrimp is counted once and then leaves the count.
  • a shrimp keeps the same strength all through the haul, so the weak ones break early.

Numbers it uses

How strength varies between shrimpspread 0.3 on a log scale (0.2 to 0.45)Borrowedcrab claws, Palmer, Taylor and Barton 1999 (free copy), pp. 284 to 285

What it can't do here

It does not say how badly a shrimp is hurt.

Best estimate and field checksHow the five field studies weight the 192 versions

Our best estimate, and how the field studies shape it

Each of the 192 versions gets a weight for how well it matches five field studies of small hauls: 1 if its average sits inside every field figure, falling towards 0 the further outside it lands. The best estimate is the middle of the 192 results, each counted by its weight. Model

Why the best estimate uses all five studies

It uses all five studies instead of one, and it keeps every version the studies cannot rule out, at a weight that says how well it fits. In practice the weights rest mainly on three of the studies (Noell, Fox and Salini, described under field checks below); the other two rule out almost nothing.

The stricter Salini check in the table below drops a version whenever its average crushes more than Salini et al. measured plus a margin for sampling error. It does so even when Salini's figure sits well inside that version's own spread of results. It also depends on a single haul: the 278 kg haul, the one with the least damage (9.4%), leaves the same 62 versions on its own as all three hauls together.

The field studies lean towards the lever-arm rule, a single load pattern per stage and fewer spine contacts. They say almost nothing about weakening, the lift width, the ramp load or how unevenly the load is shared.

How the weight is built, and the guesses it rests on

  1. Every version starts equally likely. Guess: we have no basis to prefer one before the field checks.
  2. Each check measures how far a version's average lies outside the field figure, in units of the model's own spread for that check (its 5th to 95th percentile width ÷ 3.29). Inside the figure the distance is zero. Guess: the model's spread is the right yardstick for how badly a miss counts.
  3. Each study counts once. Its penalty is the average squared distance over its checks, so Larssen's six checks do not outvote the others. Guess: the five studies deserve equal say.
  4. Weight = e−½ × the sum of the five penalties. A version that misses one study by one spread keeps 61% of its weight. Guess: a normal-shaped penalty.
  5. The field figures are our reading of each study (table under Field checks). Leaving Fox out moves no best estimate by more than 4 points. Leaving out Noell, the hardest check, moves the most: Norway rises from 47% to 53%.

Result: 6 versions have their average inside every field figure, 70 keep at least half their weight and 56 keep under 5%. The default version keeps 0.60.

How the best estimate relates to the default result

The default results (15% for US ocean shrimp, 8% for North Sea brown shrimp, 7% for US Gulf shrimp) come from one of the 192 versions: each unknown at our preferred option, with big hauls counting for more because they hold more shrimp. Averaged over hauls instead, the same version gives 14%, 7% and 6%. The best estimate is higher, at 25%, 13% and 13%, because many versions that crush more, such as four load patterns per stage or a narrower lifted bag, also fit the small-haul studies, and the studies cannot rule them out. The default shows what our preferred version says; the best estimate also counts what we do not know about the seven unknowns.

Only the Norwegian and Greenland fleets haul over a stern ramp in the model, so the ramp load changes nothing elsewhere. What each unknown means for a shrimp in the bag is explained card by card under What moves the numbers most.

How it was checked against the real world

We found no study that scored crushed or pierced shells straight out of a shrimp codend, so every comparison is indirect. We scored all 192 versions against five field studies of small hauls (19 to 390 kg per codend) that count damaged or dead animals after a trawl. Each study gives a field figure the model should not exceed (Fox also a lower one). A version is ruled out by a figure only if even its 5th percentile lies above it (for Fox's lower figure, only if even its 95th percentile lies below it). The fit weights behind the best estimate come from these checks. Nothing in the model was tuned to fit them.

The stricter check (a version's average must stay under the share plus two standard errors) keeps 62, and the 278 kg haul alone sets that cut.

Its grade also counts intact soft-shelled prawns, so it can only say the model is too high.

Not ruled out by any of the five: 112 of the 192 versions.

Every one of these checks is weak. Each comes from a different species or fishery, most count more than crushing (any damage, or death), and most can only show that the model is too high. Crushed shrimp may survive, so the two studies that count deaths (Larssen and Broadhurst) are poor ceilings on crushing; they rule out only 2 and 0 versions, so the best estimate barely rests on them. That is why we weight the versions by all five instead of letting any one of them cut.

What moves the numbers mostEach unknown, what it changes, and by how much

What moves the numbers most, and how

For each unknown: what it changes for a shrimp in the bag, at which stage, the share crushed before and after for Norway, and the change in every fishery. Each change starts from the default settings and keeps everything else fixed, so the "after" share is approximate. Under each card, the same unknown measured across all 192 versions. Model

Unknown · load patterns per stage

If the pile rearranges four times at each stage instead of once

What changes
Each shrimp gets an uneven-load factor: how much more or less than its share of the load it carries. With one pattern it gets one draw per stage. With four, the pile is taken to shift four times as the bag is hauled, tipped and lifted, so each shrimp gets four fresh draws, and it is crushed if any one of them is too much.
Where
Every stage, but it matters where loads are already close to shell strength: the ramp and the lift in big catches.
Why it is unknown
We found no observation of how a packed codend rearranges during a haul.
What could settle it
Video of the codend while it is hauled in. A computer simulation that follows every prawn in a pile could also test it, though it would need checking against real observations.
47%→≈81%Norway, 1 to 4 patterns

Unknown · force rule

If force reaches a shrimp only where neighbours touch it

What changes
The default rule turns slice pressure into force through the shrimp's estimated side area. The lever-arm rule passes the force through the few points where neighbours touch it, which works out at a smaller effective area: for a northern prawn 4.2 instead of 6.3 cm², so about two-thirds of the force on every shrimp.
Where
Every stage equally, because it scales every force.
Why it is unknown
We found no measurement of the force on a single shrimp inside a pressed pile.
What could settle it
A computer simulation of a pile could estimate the force on one prawn against the slice pressure, though it would need checking against real observations.
47%→≈23%Norway, area rule to lever arm

Unknown · weakening

If a shell held under load slowly gets weaker

What changes
The weakening option treats the 17 N starting figure as a load lasting about 5 seconds (2 to 10, our judgement). With weakening on, a shell held under load for minutes or hours breaks at a lower force, as mussel shell, bone and insect cuticle do. The model then follows simulated shrimp through the haul and adds up the damage.
Where
The long stages: hours of tow and the time on deck. It matters most where a long load sits just under shell strength.
Why it is unknown
We found no test of this on a crustacean shell.
What could settle it
Published load-duration tests on crustacean cuticle, if any exist; a literature search, not a new test.
47%→≈63%Norway, weakening off to on

Unknown · ramp load

If only the slope of the ramp presses on the catch

What changes
By default the bag lying on the ramp and deck is taken to be as deep as half its towed width, an upper bound because a real bag flattens. The other option counts only the share of the weight that the slope presses into the catch.
Where
The ramp, so only the two stern-trawler fisheries. The others have no ramp and don't move.
Why it is unknown
We found no film or source that lets us measure a ramp angle or how flat the bag lies.
What could settle it
Photos or video of the bag on the ramp with something of known size in view.
47%→≈29%Norway, full depth to slope only

Unknown · lift width

If the hanging bag narrows to half its towed width

What changes
The same catch in a narrower bag stands taller, so the bottom slices carry more weight above them.
Where
The lift only. It matters most where the lift is the main load: fisheries that lift the bag over the side, such as US ocean shrimp and Argentina.
Why it is unknown
We found no measurement of a hanging codend's shape.
What could settle it
Photos of the bag hanging from the crane, with something of known size in view.
15%→≈37%US ocean shrimp, full to half width (Norway 47% → about 59%)

Unknown · spine rule

If more shrimp have a neighbour's spine pressing on them

What changes
A spine tip pressing end-on can pierce a shell at a small fraction of the force a broad squeeze needs. The default gives 7% of shrimp a spine tip carrying 35% of their load; the other rule gives 20% of shrimp a spine tip carrying 40%.
Where
Every stage. It matters most for big penaeids such as Argentine red shrimp, whose broad shells are strong but can still be pierced.
Why it is unknown
We found no observation of how shrimp lie against each other inside a real pile.
What could settle it
Counting pierced shells in catch that is already landed. A computer simulation with spines on every prawn could also help, though it would need checking against real observations.
47%→≈56%Norway, fewer to more spine contacts

Unknown · uneven load

How unevenly a pile shares its load

What changes
The shape of the uneven-load factor. Shape 1 is very uneven: a few shrimp carry many times their share. Shape 4 is fairly even. Shape 2, the default, is in between. It comes from flat plastic discs.
Where
Every stage.
Why it is unknown
We found no measurement of it for shrimp.
What could settle it
A computer simulation of a pile, checked against real observations.

Not one of the seven · moult season

A bad moult season, with many more soft shells

What changes
Freshly moulted shrimp break at a fifth of the force of a hard shell. This scenario raises the share of soft-shelled cold-water prawns from 1.5% to 10%, and half-hard ones from 10% to 55%.
Where
Only the cold-water prawn fisheries (Greenland, Norway, US ocean shrimp). The others keep their own moult inputs, so they don't move.
What could settle it
Moult records from fishery surveys (for example ODFW for ocean shrimp, IMR for Norway).
47%→≈65%Norway, default to a bad moult season

This is not one of the seven unknowns. It shows what a bad moulting season would do.

Not one of the seven · how the pile fills the bag

If the catch fills the whole bag loosely

What changes
Instead of a packed heap at the back, the catch is spread loosely through the whole part of the bag where catch collects. Each slice then holds fewer shrimp, so each shrimp carries more of the slice's pressure.
Where
Every stage.
What could settle it
Codend video, or tank tests of how catch fills a codend.
47%→≈55%Norway, packed heap to loose fill

This is not one of the seven unknowns.

Between them, the load-pattern and force-rule unknowns span about 22% to 80% for Norway (our model estimate). Settling them needs measurements of how load is shared and rearranged inside a packed bag. The one-at-a-time changes come from a separate run of the model; the "across all 192" lines come from the same run as the dot chart.

Alive at the killing stepThe closest measurements of how many shrimp are still alive

Alive at the killing step

Our crushing model stops before this step, and we found no study that counts all kept shrimp, alive and dead, just before the cooker, freezer or stunner. These are the closest measurements we found. They cover different temperatures, times in air and tow lengths.

In plain words

  • Warm air harms shrimp quickly; cold air much more slowly. At 23 to 30 °C most Gulf shrimp no longer appeared normal after 15 minutes in air (impaired, not counted as dead), and dry-sorted seabob went from about half alive to almost none in 16 minutes. In cold air, northern prawn kept 80 to 90% survival after 15 minutes.
  • Warm water adds to the deaths of northern prawn. In an August catch, half were dead about 15 minutes after the haul, after a 2.5-hour tow; the authors also blame moulting, so warmth is not the only cause.
  • For cold-water catches, tow length may matter too. In the March observations none were dead after 2.5 h tows. After 10 h tows about a third were dead, but they were first counted 3 h after hauling, so the effects of towing and of the later handling cannot be separated.
  • Freshly moulted shrimp died far more often. After sorting, 72% of just-moulted brown shrimp were dead, against 15% of hard-shelled ones.
